﴿Yā ayyuhā al-muzzammil﴾ (O you who are wrapped up). This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). The pattern (wazn) of al-muzzammil is mutafa''il (mutaf''il), so its original form was mutazammil. Then the ta' was made quiescent and assimilated (idgham) into the zay.

Regarding calling the Prophet (ﷺ) "al-muzzammil," there are three opinions. The first is that at the time the verse was revealed he was wrapped in a cloak or a blanket. Tazammul means wrapping oneself in garments by drawing them up and close. This is the view of Aisha and the majority of scholars. The second is that he had wrapped himself in his garments for prayer. The third is that the meaning is "the one who girds himself for prophethood," that is, the one who exerts himself and is earnest in its matter. The first is the correct view, because of what is related in al-Bukhari and Muslim: "When the angel came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the cave of Hira at the beginning of the revelation, he (ﷺ) returned to Khadijah with his muscles trembling, and said: 'Wrap me, wrap me,' so the verse 'O you who are wrapped up (al-mudaththir)' was revealed." On this basis, "O you who are wrapped up (al-muzzammil)" was also revealed, so al-muzzammil here means that he wrapped himself because of the terror that struck him when Jibril first came to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He was sleeping in a woolen cover, so he was addressed, "O you who are wrapped up," to make clear the state he was in of being wrapped in the cover, since that is a cause of heavy sleep which prevents the night prayer. But this view is remote and not sound.

Al-Suhayli said: In addressing him as al-muzzammil there are two benefits. The first is gentleness, for when the Arabs intend to be gentle with the one addressed, they call him by a name derived from the state he is in, like the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Ali: "Get up, Abu Turab" (father of dust). The second benefit is an alert to every wrapped-up sleeper at night, so that he may awaken to the remembrance of Allah, because a name derived from a verb is shared by the one addressed and by everyone who has that attribute.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 73, verse 2–4:

﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾. Scholars differ over whether this command to stand in prayer at night (qiyam al-layl) is obligatory (wajib) or recommended (mandub). According to the view that it is recommended, the ruling is established and not abrogated (mansukh). As for the view that it is obligatory, there are three opinions. The first is that it was an obligation upon the Prophet ﷺ alone, and it remained obligatory for him until he died. The second is that it was obligatory upon him and his community, so they stood [in prayer] until their feet swelled; then it was abrogated by His words at the end of the surah: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer]﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and it became voluntary (tatawwu'). This is the view of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and it is the sound one. There is disagreement as to how long it remained obligatory: ʿĀʾishah said one year; it was also said eight months, and it was said ten years. According to this view, the abrogating verse is Medinan. The third is that it was obligatory upon the Prophet ﷺ and his community, and it is established and not abrogated, but the whole night is not required; rather, only what is easy of it (ma tayassara minhu). This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin.

﴿Except a little, half of it, or reduce from it a little, or add to it﴾. Regarding the meaning of this statement there are four opinions. The first, which is the most well-known and the most apparent, is that the exception is from the night, and His words "half of it" are either a substitute (badal) for "the night" or for "a little"; and half is considered little in relation to the whole. The two pronouns in "or reduce from it" and "or add to it" refer to the half. The meaning is that Allah gave him the choice between three states: that he stand half the night, or reduce from the half a little, or add to it. The second: al-Zamakhshari said, "except a little" is an exception from the half, as if He said: "half the night except a little." Thus, according to this, He gave him the choice between two states: that he stand for less than half or more than half. This is weak, because His words "or reduce from it a little" already imply reducing from the half, so there is no additional benefit in excepting a little from the half. The third opinion, also stated by al-Zamakhshari: it is possible that by His words "or reduce from it a little" He means half of the half, which is a quarter, and the pronoun in His words "or add to it" returns to that, i.e., add to the quarter so that it becomes a third. Thus the choice according to this is between standing for half, a third, or a quarter. This is also remote. The fourth, stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah: it is possible that the meaning of "except a little" is the nights in which an excuse prevents him from standing [in prayer], and the intended meaning of "the night" here is "the nights," so it is a collective noun (jins). This is remote, because the excepted "little" has already been explained by what follows: half the night, or reducing from it, or adding to it. This indicates that the intended night in the exception is a part of the parts of the night, not a part of the nights. If it is asked: Why did He restrict the reduction from the half by "a little," saying "or reduce from it a little," but leave the addition unrestricted, saying "or add to it" without "a little"? The answer: in addition, abundance is fitting, so He did not restrict it by littleness, unlike reduction; for if He had left reduction unrestricted, it would have allowed that one reduce from the half a great deal.

﴿And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation (tartil)﴾. Tartil is deliberateness, prolonging (madd), giving the vowels their full length (ishbaʿ al-harakat), and clarifying the letters. This aids reflection upon the meanings of the Qur'an, unlike hadhr (rapid, careless recitation) whose reciter does not understand what he says. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to separate his recitation letter by letter, and he would not pass a verse of mercy without stopping and asking, nor pass a verse of punishment without stopping and seeking refuge [with Allah].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 73, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, We will bestow upon you a heavy word.﴾ This verse is a parenthetical interjection between the verse on the night prayer (qiyam al-layl), and the "heavy word" is the Qur'an. Scholars differed about describing it as heavy in five opinions. The first: it was called "heavy" because of the hardship the Prophet (ﷺ) experienced when revelation descended upon him, to the extent that his forehead would drip with sweat on a very cold day. His body, peace be upon him, would become heavy by this, so much so that when revelation came to him while he was on his she-camel, she would kneel down under him, and when revelation came to him while his thigh was upon the thigh of Zayd ibn Thabit, it nearly crushed Zayd's thigh. According to this view, the heaviness is literal. The second: it is heavy upon the disbelievers because of its inimitability and its warning. The third: it is heavy in the balance (on the Day of Judgment). The fourth: it is speech that has weight and eminence. The fifth: it is heavy because of what it contains of obligations, commands and prohibitions, and this is the choice of Ibn 'Atiyyah. According to this, the interjection with this verse suits the night prayer, because of its difficulty.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 73, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, the rising at night (nashi'at al-layl)﴾ There are seven opinions concerning nashi'a. The first is that it means the soul that rises at night, i.e., that rises from its bed and stands in prayer. The second is the groups that rise at night to pray. The third is worship that arises at night, i.e., that occurs during it. The fourth is that nashi'a is standing after sleep, so whoever stands at the beginning of the night before sleeping has not stood in nashi'a. The fifth is that nashi'a is standing at the beginning of the night after 'Isha'. The sixth is nashi'a after Maghrib and 'Isha'. The seventh is that nashi'at al-layl refers to all of the night's hours. ﴿It is firmer in tread (ashaddu wat'an)﴾. This may carry two meanings. One is that it is heavier and more difficult for the one praying; from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, make Your tread heavy upon Mudar." The heavier also means greater in reward, so the meaning is an exhortation to stand in prayer at night because of the abundance of reward. The second meaning is that it is firmer in standing, owing to solitude, presence of mind, and distance from people. This is close in meaning to ﴿more upright in speech (aqwamu qīlan)﴾. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read wiṭā' with a kasra on the waw, on the pattern fi'āl, and its meaning is conformity: that is, the heart conforms with the tongue through presence of mind.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 73, verses 7–9:

﴿Indeed, for you by day is extensive occupation (sabh tawil).﴾ Al-sabh here means being occupied with one's affairs (al-tasarruf fi al-ishtighal). The meaning is: the day is sufficient for you to attend to your affairs, and you should be free at night to worship your Lord. It was also said: the meaning is that if you miss anything of the night prayer, then make it up during the day, for the day is long and has room for that.

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾. It was said: its meaning is, say: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful" at the beginning of your prayer. But the wording is more general than that.

﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾. That is, cut yourself off towards Him through worship and by relying upon Him alone. It was also said: tabattul (tabattul, devotion) is the renunciation of worldly life. Tabtilan (tabtilan, complete devotion) is a verbal noun (masdar) that does not follow the regular pattern (ala ghayr qiyas).

﴿So take Him as your Trustee (wakil).﴾ The wakil (wakil, trustee) is the one who manages affairs and to whom matters are entrusted. So this is a command to put one's trust in Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 73, verses 10–14:**

﴿And bear patiently what they say﴾. That is, what the disbelievers say. The verse is *mansukha* (abrogated, its ruling superseded) by the sword. It was also said that what is abrogated is only the conciliation (*muhadana*, a truce or accommodation) implied by His saying ﴿and forsake them with a gracious forsaking﴾. As for patience, it is commanded at every time.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾. This is a threat against them. "The deniers" (*al-mukadhdhibin*) is in the accusative, either as an object with a companion particle (*ma'a*) or as a conjunct.

﴿Leave Me with the deniers, possessors of luxury﴾. That is, the luxury (*al-tan'um*) of this world. It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning the Banu al-Mughira, a people of Quraysh who were affluent in this world.

﴿Fetters﴾. Plural of *nikl*, which is an iron shackle. It is narrated that they are black fetters of fire.

﴿And food that chokes﴾. This is the tree of *zaqqum*. The meaning of *dha ghussa* is that those who eat it choke on it. It was also said that it is thorns that lodge in their throats, neither going down nor coming out. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse and fainted.

﴿On the day the earth quakes﴾. That is, it shakes and convulses. The governing element (*al-'amil*) of "day" is the meaning of the preceding statement, namely ﴿Indeed, with Us are fetters﴾.

﴿And the mountains will be like heaps of sand, poured out﴾. *Al-kathib* is a heap of sand. *Al-mahil* is soft, loose [sand] that the wind scatters, i.e., spreads out; its form (*wazn*) is that of a passive participle (*maf'ul*). The meaning is that the mountains, when they are blown away on the Day of Resurrection, become like a heap of sand.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 73, verses 10–14:**

﴿And bear patiently what they say﴾. That is, what the disbelievers say. The verse is *mansukha* (abrogated, its ruling superseded) by the sword. It was also said that what is abrogated is only the conciliation (*muhadana*, a truce or accommodation) implied by His saying ﴿and forsake them with a gracious forsaking﴾. As for patience, it is commanded at every time.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾. This is a threat against them. "The deniers" (*al-mukadhdhibin*) is in the accusative, either as an object with a companion particle (*ma'a*) or as a conjunct.

﴿Leave Me with the deniers, possessors of luxury﴾. That is, the luxury (*al-tan'um*) of this world. It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning the Banu al-Mughira, a people of Quraysh who were affluent in this world.

﴿Fetters﴾. Plural of *nikl*, which is an iron shackle. It is narrated that they are black fetters of fire.

﴿And food that chokes﴾. This is the tree of *zaqqum*. The meaning of *dha ghussa* is that those who eat it choke on it. It was also said that it is thorns that lodge in their throats, neither going down nor coming out. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse and fainted.

﴿On the day the earth quakes﴾. That is, it shakes and convulses. The governing element (*al-'amil*) of "day" is the meaning of the preceding statement, namely ﴿Indeed, with Us are fetters﴾.

﴿And the mountains will be like heaps of sand, poured out﴾. *Al-kathib* is a heap of sand. *Al-mahil* is soft, loose [sand] that the wind scatters, i.e., spreads out; its form (*wazn*) is that of a passive participle (*maf'ul*). The meaning is that the mountains, when they are blown away on the Day of Resurrection, become like a heap of sand.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 73, verses 15–16:

﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger﴾ — an address to all of mankind, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent to people in their entirety. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an address to the people of Makkah.

﴿as a witness over you﴾ — that is, he bears witness over your deeds, of disbelief and faith, obedience and disobedience. He bears witness only over those he has encountered, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will say what my brother Jesus said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them﴾" [al-Ma'idah: 117].

﴿as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ — meaning Musa (peace be upon him), and this is what is intended by His saying: ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾. So the definite article (al-lam) is for a previously known referent (lam al-'ahd).

﴿a severe seizing﴾ — that is, a great and harsh seizing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 73, verses 17–19:

﴿How then will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will make the children grey-haired?﴾ "Yawman" (a day) is the object (maf'ul bihi), and its governing verb is "tattaqun" (you guard against). That is: how will you guard yourselves against the Day of Resurrection and its terrors, if you disbelieve? It is also said that it is the object, on the basis that "kafartum" means "jahadtum" (you denied). It is also said that it is an adverbial of time (zarf), meaning: how will you have taqwa (guarding of oneself against God's displeasure) on the Day of Resurrection? It is also possible that the governing element is omitted, its estimated sense being: remember His saying, ﴿the sky will be split asunder by it﴾, ﴿will make the children grey-haired﴾. "Al-Wildan" is the plural of "walid," which is the young child. "Al-Shayb," with a kasra on the shin, is the plural of "ashyab," and its pattern is fu'ul, with the fa' vowelled with a damma but given a kasra because of the yā'. "Yaj'alu" may be taken as having God (Exalted is He) or the Day as its subject. The meaning is that the children will turn grey on the Day of Resurrection. It is said that this is literal, and it is said that it is an expression for the severity of that Day, and it is said that it is an expression for its length. ﴿the sky will be split asunder by it﴾: "Al-infitar" means splitting apart (al-inshiqaq), and the pronoun in the genitive ("bihi") refers back to the Day, meaning: the sky will be split apart because of its severity. It is also possible that it refers back to God, that the sky will be split apart by His command and power. The first is more apparent. "Al-sama'" (sky) is feminine, and "munfatir" appears in the masculine because its femininity is not real, or because it is in the construct sense, estimated as "dhat infitar" (possessing splitting), or because he meant the ceiling (al-saqf). ﴿His promise is always fulfilled﴾: the pronoun in "wa'duhu" may refer back to the Day or to God, and the first is more apparent, because it is explicitly mentioned. ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾: the reference is to the preceding admonitions and warnings. ﴿So whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾: he means the way of drawing near to God, and the meaning of the statement is an urging toward this and an encouragement to it.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 73, verse 20:

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) for almost two-thirds of the night﴾. This verse was revealed to abrogate (naskh) what was commanded at the beginning of the surah concerning the night prayer. Its meaning is that Allah knows you and those Muslims with you stand in prayer in varying amounts, sometimes more and sometimes less, because you cannot calculate and precisely determine the times of the night, and only Allah can do that. So He lightened it for you and commanded you to recite what is easy of the Qur'an. ﴿and half of it and a third of it﴾. Whoever reads "wa-nisfihi wa-thuluthihi" with the genitive (bi-l-khafd) treats it as coordinated with thuluthay al-layl (two-thirds of the night), meaning you stand for less than two-thirds of the night and less than its half and its third. Whoever reads with the accusative (bi-l-nasb) treats it as coordinated with adna (nearly), meaning you stand for nearly two-thirds of the night, and you stand for its half at times and its third at other times. ﴿and a group﴾ refers to the Muslims, and it is coordinated with the subject pronoun in taqumu (you stand). ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾: the pronoun refers to what is understood from the context of the speech, meaning you will not be able to count the measure of the night. It has also been said that the meaning is: you will not be able to bear it, that is, you will not be able to stand the whole night. ﴿So He turned to you in forgiveness﴾ is an expression for the lightening (of the obligation), like His saying: ﴿So since you did not do it, and Allah has turned to you in forgiveness﴾ [al-Mujadila: 13]. ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, meaning: if you are unable to stand the whole night, then stand for part of it, and recite in your prayer at night what is easy of the Qur'an. This command is for recommendation (nadb). Ibn 'Atiyya said: according to the majority of scholars, it is for permissibility (ibahah).

A group, including al-Hasan (al-Basri) and Ibn Sirin, said: it is an obligation that cannot be dispensed with, even if only the minimum possible. Some of them even said: whoever prays the witr has fulfilled this command. It has also been said that it was obligatory and then abrogated by the five daily prayers. Some of them said: it is obligatory upon the people of the Qur'an (ahl al-Qur'an) only, and not upon others. ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾: In this verse Allah mentions the excuses that occur to human beings and prevent them from standing in the night prayer. Among them is illness, and among them is travel for trade, which is ﴿striking through the earth seeking of Allah's bounty﴾, and among them is jihad. Then He repeated the command to recite what is easy, either to emphasize the command to do so or to emphasize the lightening. This latter view is more evident, because He mentioned it right after the excuses. ﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾ means the obligatory prayers. ﴿And lend to Allah a good loan﴾ means give charity. It has been mentioned in al-Baqarah [45]. ﴿Whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward﴾: khayran is in the accusative because it is the second object of tajidu (you will find), and the pronoun (huwa) is a separator (dami'r al-fasl). ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾. Some scholars said that seeking forgiveness after the prayer is derived from this verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek forgiveness three times when he finished his prayer.
